books.section: Topic 4.5 Market Revolution: Economic Transformations, D. Regional Specialization
The North and the Textile Industry

stimulus.text: "From whence originated the idea, that it was derogatory to a lady's dignity, or a blot upon the female character, to labor? . . . Homer tells us of princesses who used to draw water from the springs, and wash with their own hands the finest of the linen of their respective families. The famous Lucretia used to spin in the midst of her attendants; and the wife of Ulysses, after the siege of Troy, employed herself in weaving, until her husband returned to Ithaca. . . . Few American fortunes will support a woman who is above the calls of her family. . . . To be able to earn one's own living by laboring with the hands, should be reckoned among female accomplishments." — "Dignity of Labor," The Lowell Offering, 1842
stimulus.source_note: "Dignity of Labor," The Lowell Offering, 1842; wording verified against the Project Gutenberg text of Mind Amongst the Spindles (Lowell Offering selections) and the CrackAP transcription. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The author lists princesses, Lucretia, and the wife of Ulysses mainly to show that

options.text: women in ancient times held political power equal to men
options.misconception: The essay never claims ancient women ruled; it talks about their work, not their power.

options.text: American women should refuse factory work and return to farm life
options.misconception: The author defends earning a living by hand labor; she never tells women to leave the mills.

options.text: manual labor has long been compatible with a woman's dignity
factory work was the first time women had ever labored with their hands
options.misconception: The examples prove the opposite: women labored with their hands long before factories existed.

rationales.A: The princesses draw water and wash linen; none of that is ruling. The essay is about work, not power.
rationales.B: The last line calls earning a living by hand labor an accomplishment. That praises mill work, not rejection of it.
rationales.C: Each example is a respected woman doing manual work: a princess drawing water, Lucretia spinning, Penelope weaving. If they kept their dignity while laboring, so can a mill girl.
rationales.D: The whole list exists to show women have always labored. Factory work is new; women's hand labor is not.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what the examples have in common. Every one is a woman of high standing doing manual work.
2. Ask what that proves. If princesses and Lucretia kept their dignity while spinning and weaving, labor itself cannot be degrading.
3. Connect it to Lowell. The essay answers the charge that mill work shamed a woman, using old examples to defend a new life.
Background: The Lowell Offering was written by the young women working in the Lowell textile mills in the 1840s.
Remember: when an author piles up old examples, ask what new claim they are all meant to support.
